heard: Soviet orbital satellites once confirmed an incoming nuclear strike with highest reliability. On September 26, 1983, early warning screens alerted duty officer Stanislav Petrov to five American missiles. With impact minutes away, computers insisted an attack was underway. Yet Petrov suspected a real American strike would be an overwhelming barrage, not five isolated launches. Ground radar showed clear skies, confirming his suspicion. Petrov decided against reporting an attack, alerting headquarters instead that the system had malfunctioned. Investigations revealed satellites encountered a rare solar alignment. Blinded by the glare, the sensors mistook sunlight, reflecting off high-altitude clouds for missile launches. Glinting sunlight bouncing off clouds had triggered humanity's closest nuclear false alarm.
